claim: Commonly used binary classification accuracy metrics—including the increasingly popular Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC)—are not actually independent of class prevalence or reference standard quality, so their apparent values can seriously misrepresent true classifier performance.
method: The authors analyze and run simulations with realistic prevalence ranges and varying levels of imperfect reference standards (as found in fields like remote sensing and medicine) to compute apparent values of metrics such as recall, precision, specificity, NPV, J, F1, likelihood ratios, and MCC, comparing them to true accuracy.
result: They show that all examined metrics, including MCC, shift substantially in magnitude and even direction depending on prevalence and reference standard imperfections, and that a classifier with essentially random (coin-toss) skill can yield a deceptively high apparent MCC.

verdict:
The claim overlaps very substantially with source [1], "Challenges in the real world use of classification accuracy metrics: From recall and precision to the Matthews correlation coefficient" (2023). The abstract of [1] explicitly states that apparent accuracy can differ greatly from true accuracy due to variations in prevalence and use of an imperfect reference standard, and that it covers recall, precision, and the MCC specifically—this is essentially the same thesis, scope of metrics, and framing (prevalence + reference standard quality) as the claim under evaluation. Source [2], "Ground Truth in Classification Accuracy Assessment: Myth and Reality" (2024), also overlaps significantly: it explicitly discusses the false assumption of a perfect ground reference dataset, uses simulations of realistic scenarios, and examines effects of reference quality and class abundance on apparent accuracy—closely matching the METHOD and RESULT described in the claim.

Given this, the claim does not appear to be novel; it strongly resembles prior work by what is likely the same research program or authors, extending or reiterating findings already published in [1] and [2]. The specific mention of MCC and coin-toss classifiers yielding deceptively high apparent MCC could be an incremental addition, but the core argument—that prevalence and reference standard imperfections distort apparent accuracy metrics including MCC—is already present in [1]. The other retrieved sources ([3]–[7]) are unrelated or only tangentially relevant (annotation reliability, unrelated ML applications) and do not inform novelty assessment. Overall: significant overlap with [1] and [2], not insufficient evidence.
